units.summary: Rabbi Asi reports seeing Rabbi Yoḥanan eat Samaritan slaughter, which leads Rabbi Zeira to resolve his doubt regarding whether a specific decree was accepted.
Rabbi Meir sends Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar to fetch wine from Samaritans, but an old man intercepts him with a warning that leads to a change in legal status.
Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Yosef is sent by Rabbi Abbahu to get wine but is warned by an elder, leading to a chain of reports that results in Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi declaring Samaritans as gentiles.
Rabbi Zeira and Rav Asi visit an inn where Rav Asi eats eggs cooked in wine; Rabbi Zeira initially worries Rav Asi sinned but investigates and finds a legal justification.

After hearing testimony that Rabbi Meir ate untithed produce in Beit She'an, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permits the region's produce, leading to a confrontation with his family which he resolves through a biblical interpretation.
While on a mission to redeem captives, Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya’ir commands the Ginai River to part for him and his companions, which it eventually does three times.

Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya’ir arrives at an inn where his donkey refuses to eat the barley provided by the hosts. Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya’ir's donkey refuses to eat until its food is properly tithed by the hosts.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi invites Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya’ir to dine, but Pineḥas ultimately refuses due to the presence of dangerous mules, ending in a supernatural separation.
A woman tries to perform sorcery against Rabbi Ḥanina by taking dust from under his feet, but he tells her it will not work because only God has power.
An incident involving a bird with a displaced windpipe was brought before the Sages, who ruled that any uncertainty in slaughter results in invalidity.
Rav Yosef disqualified thirteen animals after discovering his knife was notched upon completing the final slaughter.
A Tanna recites a legal ruling regarding cooking on Shabbat before Rav, who then silences him.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak reports that a Tanna recited a law about slaughtering on Shabbat before Rav, who then challenged the Tanna's logic.
The Gemara concludes a discussion from the previous page regarding Rav silencing a tanna who recited a specific ruling about slaughtering on Shabbat.
The Gemara discusses a tanna reciting a baraita before Rav regarding slaughtering on Shabbat and the subsequent legal debate between Rabbi and Rabbi Ḥiyya.
Rav Pappa describes a case where one person binds another and diverts water onto him, causing his death, to define the legal status of direct force.
Shmuel's father repeatedly notched knives in various ways and sent them from Babylonia to the Land of Israel to receive a definitive ruling on which types of notches disqualify a knife for slaughter.
While Ravina and Rav Aha were sitting before Rav Ashi, a knife was brought for inspection, and Rav Ashi had Rav Aha perform the physical examination to demonstrate the correct procedure.
A slaughterer is penalized by Rava bar Ḥinnana for not showing his knife, but Rav Ashi later examines the knife and reverses the ruling.
Upon moving to Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Zeira eats meat slaughtered according to a local leniency, which provokes the anger of his former teacher Rav Yosef when he hears of it.
Resh Lakish permits a certain type of slaughter and Rabbi Yoḥanan comments on his leniency.
Rav Nahman validates a specific type of slaughter and, when challenged on his source, responds that he does not know specific names but knows the tradition.
After Rav Huna rules stringently on a case where Rav Yehuda ruled leniently, Rav Yehuda becomes angry, leading Rav Hisda to advise Rav Huna on whether to retract.
Rav Nahman arrives in Sura and is asked a legal question regarding the validity of a specific slaughtering technique.
Rabbi Abba observes a legal exchange between Rav Kahana and Rav Yehuda and subsequently travels to Eretz Yisrael to report these rulings to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yohanan.
When Rabbi Zeira arrived in Eretz Yisrael, he challenged Rabbi Ami's teaching on pinching, causing Rabbi Ami to be momentarily stunned before refining his position.
The Gemara records that Rabbi Hanina, even at the age of eighty, was physically capable of standing on one leg to remove and put on his shoes.
Rav Geviha from Bei Katil travels to Rav Ashi to challenge a legal ruling regarding the purification of temed.
A Roman official challenges Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai on the origin of birds, leading the rabbi to give a superficial answer to the official and a deeper explanation to his confused students.
A bloody duck is brought to Rava's house, prompting a dilemma about whether its simanim were damaged before slaughter.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta enters a butcher shop and takes meat from a bull slaughtered with multiple cuts to demonstrate its validity, prompting a comment from Rabbi Zeira.
Rava examines an arrow for Rabbi Yona bar Taḥlifa and then successfully slaughters a bird in flight with it.
Rava, suspecting Rav Nahman was merely deflecting his legal objection, went out to investigate and discovered a baraita that confirmed Rav Nahman's position.
When Rav Kahana and Rav Asi question Rav on the specifics of an interruption in slaughter, Rav explains he was never bold enough with his uncle, Rabbi Hiyya, to ask for such clarification.
On the day Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya was appointed Nasi in Yavne, Rabbi Akiva expounded on the laws of ritual impurity in earthenware vessels.
After Rav's death, Shmuel encounters Rav's students and asks them to clarify Rav's ruling regarding an animal in danger of imminent death.
A healthy man orders a divorce for his wife and then immediately climbs a roof and falls to his death, leading to a debate on his intent.
Arabs in Tzikuneya gave rams to Jewish slaughterers while declaring the blood and fat were for idols, prompting a legal inquiry to Rav Yosef.
An animal with a suspected predator wound is brought to Rabba, who begins inspecting it from the outside until Abaye challenges him with his own legal ruling.

After Rava rules a bull belonging to Rav Ukva's sons is a tereifa due to a complex slaughtering issue, Rabbi Abba hears of the case, declares the bull kosher, and orders Rava to compensate the owners.
A bull belonging to Rav Ukva's sons is slaughtered in a questionable manner, leading to a strict ruling by Rava that is eventually overturned by Rabbi Abba, who orders financial compensation.
When an animal with a cut windpipe was brought to Rav, his students challenged his inspection method, leading Rabba bar bar Hana to permit and eat the meat.
Rabba's wife (daughter of Rav Hisda) questions him for buying meat from an animal he himself permitted, and he explains why it doesn't look like a conflict of interest.
Rabbi Elazar consistently refused gifts and invitations from the Nasi's household, citing the verse that one who hates gifts shall live.
Rabbi Yirmeya inspects a bird and finds bean-like protrusions on its skull.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Yosef reports Rav's ruling to Shmuel, who dismisses Rav's knowledge of the subject.
Rav Natan bar Avin checks both the membrane and nerve tissue of a spinal cord while sitting before Rav, who tells him the second check is unnecessary.
While in a bathhouse, Levi sees a man strike his head and remarks that the man's brain tissue has been fatally compromised.
Rav Dimi bar Yitzḥak asks Rabbi Yehuda for a physical demonstration of a spinal boundary; after Rav Dimi brings a kid for the purpose, Rabbi Yehuda decides to teach him the verbal tradition instead.
Ulla recounts how Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi was inspecting an injured bird but was interrupted by a messenger from the Nasi and left before Ulla could see the conclusion.
When an army arrived in Pumbedita, Rabba and Rav Yosef fled and were met by Rabbi Zeira, who shared a legal tradition with them.
A man brings a lung with an extra lobe to Mareimar, who deems it kosher; Rav Aha intercepts the man at the door and sends him back to clarify the ruling.
When Rav Ashi intends to rule a lung with an extra lobe as non-kosher, Rav Huna Mar bar Avya informs him that such a feature is common in field-grazing animals, leading to a kosher ruling.
Rabbi Natan recounts traveling overseas and advising a woman whose sons died from circumcision to wait until the child's blood was properly absorbed.
Rabbi Natan relates a second incident in Cappadocia where he diagnosed a 'green' child to prevent a third circumcision death.
While Rabbi Hananya was sick, Rabbi Natan and other scholars visited him and presented a liquefied lung, which Hananya ruled was kosher.
The residents of Asia Minor traveled to the Sanhedrin in Yavne three times regarding worm-infested livers until they finally received a ruling of permissibility.
Rav Neḥemya son of Rav Yosef physically examined a lung by inflating it in tepid water to check for leaks.
While walking through the market, Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Yosef points out cystic lungs to Rabbi Yirmeya to discern his ruling based on whether he would eat the meat.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi pass through the Tiberias market and observe lungs with hard growths without objecting to their sale.
A lung with a needle is shuttled between Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha, both of whom face objections from Rabbi Yirmeya until Rabbi Ami eventually rules it non-kosher.
A needle is found in a lung's bronchus and brought to the Sages, who refuse to issue a ruling because it conflicts with their established traditions.
Mar son of Rav Yosef intends to rule a liver with a needle as treifa until Rav Ashi challenges him with a logical comparison to flesh.
When Huna Mar and Rav Adda bar Minyumi disagreed over a needle found in a liver, they brought the case to Ravina, who ruled it kosher.
Rav Ashi recalls Rav Kahana explaining how a date pit found in a gallbladder arrived there via the connecting ducts.
A case of an animal with a perforation sealed by non-kosher fat is brought to Rava, who rules it kosher based on Rav Sheshet's opinion and financial considerations.
Manyumin the jug maker asks Rava about honey left uncovered, and Rava permits it based on a Mishnaic ruling.
Passage B contains a distinct narrative incident involving Rav Avya and Rabbi Ami that mirrors the structure of Passage A but features different actors and a completed action.
Rabbi Hanina tells his attendant to prepare fat for him to eat, but upon seeing the attendant's hesitation, he realizes the man is a Babylonian and tells him to throw it away.
An anonymous Babylonian man travels to Eretz Yisrael specifically to verify legal traditions from Rabbi Abba.
When Rava is about to declare an animal non-kosher because test perforations don't match, his son Rav Mesharshiyya rubs the tissue until they match, leading to a kosher ruling.
Rav Avira describes his eyewitness account of a specific case involving a needle in a reticulum that was brought before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi while he was standing in the study hall.
Ravina's kid jumped through a skylight to reach barley and fell, leading Rav Ashi to rule that the animal is not a tereifa because it intentionally jumped.
A ewe in Rav Chaviva's house was observed dragging its legs, leading Rav Yeimar and Ravina to debate whether the cause was rheumatism or a spinal injury.
A bull fell and bellowed in a slaughterhouse, but Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta immediately took its meat, justifying his action to the questioning Sages by citing Rav's tradition.
A cat pursuing a hen into a room at Rav Kahana's house becomes trapped by a closing door and strikes it, leaving behind drops of venom.
A repetition of the story of the cat at Rav Kahana's house, cited within an alternative version of the Talmudic discussion.
Rav Kahana asks Rav a legal question.
A fox clawed a ewe in the bathhouse of Beit Hini, and the case was brought before the Sages to determine if it was a tereifa.
A basket of birds with uncertain status was brought to Rav, who sent them to Shmuel, who then strangled them and threw them into the river to ensure they wouldn't be eaten.
Rav Ashi's duck entered a reed thicket and emerged with blood on its throat, leading Rav Ashi to evaluate its status.
Rav Ashi recalls a case brought before Rav Kahana involving a lung that looked like a shriveled date.
The hunters of the house of Yosef would kill animals by striking the sciatic nerve and sought a ruling from Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira on whether this rendered the animal a tereifa.
The hunters of Rav Pappa bar Abba killed animals by striking the kidney and were told by Rabbi Abba that they cannot add to the list of tereifot.
Rabbi Ḥana the money changer recounts how Rabbi Yoḥanan came to him to borrow a specific coin for a measurement and prevented Ḥana from standing up in his honor.

Rabba bar bar Ḥana finds rams with shriveled lungs in the desert and brings the case to the study hall, where the Sages provide him with a physical test to determine if the condition was caused by heaven or man.
Ze’eiri travels to Neharde’a and sends a message back to the Sages retracting his previous legal ruling as an error.

Passage B is a distinct incident involving a dialogue between Rav Nachman and Rav Anan regarding the rulings of Shmuel and Rav, whereas Passage A involves Rav Hana and Rav Mattana regarding a specific hen.
Rav Hana sends an injured hen to Rav Mattana, who inspects it and deems it kosher despite the broken skull bone, leading to a legal challenge.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi sends a hen that fell into fire to Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who rules it kosher despite its green innards.
Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Yosef's hen falls into fire and is sent to Rabbi Abbahu, who rules it a tereifa.
Rabbi Simai and Rabbi Tzadok travel to Lod and stop in Ono, where they issue a legal ruling.

A Roman sees a man whose stomach ruptured after a fall and slaughters the man's son in front of him to trigger a physical reaction. A Roman man uses a deceptive trick to make a man's protruding intestines retract so he can sew him up and save his life.
A basket of birds with broken legs is brought to Rava, who inspects and permits them.
Rabbi Abba finds Rav Yirmeya bar Abba inspecting birds and they engage in a legal debate regarding Rav's rulings.
Passage B describes a specific event involving a ewe in a neighborhood and a medical intervention, which prompts a response from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, distinct from the hen incidents in Passage A.
Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta treated a hen with a dislocated femur by splinting it with a reed, and it survived for a full year.
To test a verse in Proverbs, Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta tricked an ant into misreporting shade to its colony, resulting in the colony killing the ant for its false report.
An animal with two ceca is brought to Ravina, who rules it a tereifa based on Rav Huna's principle.
Rav Ashi intends to rule an animal with a specific tube a tereifa until Rav Huna Mar bar Hiyya informs him it is common in wild animals.
Mar bar Rav Ashi tries to permit an animal with a tube based on a previous precedent, but is corrected by Rav Oshaya.
Natan bar Sheila, the head butcher of Tzippori, testifies before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi regarding the status of an animal with two intestines.
Rabbi Abbahu recounts how he once ate a shekel of asafoetida and would have lost his skin to fever had he not immediately immersed in water.
A deer is brought to the Exilarch's house and permitted by Rav, but Shmuel performs a test in an oven that reveals the deer had been bitten by a snake, saving Rav from eating poisonous meat.
A dispute arises over the fat of a karkoz goat at the Exilarch's house, leading to a ruling sent from Eretz Yisrael favoring Rav Shmuel's permissive view while maintaining respect for Rav Ahai.

The Roman Emperor mocks the comparison of God to a lion, so Rabbi Yehoshua summons a supernatural lion whose roars cause physical devastation in Rome and terrify the Emperor. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya proves to the Roman emperor that he cannot see God by showing him that he cannot even look directly at the sun.
The Roman emperor tries to prepare a meal for God, but after six months of work, a rainstorm washes it away, leading him to concede.
After the emperor's daughter mocks God as a mere carpenter, Rabbi Yehoshua encounters her performing lowly labor in the market, leading her to retract her mockery.
The moon complains about sharing greatness with the sun, leading God to diminish her size and subsequently offer various compensations and a sacrificial atonement to appease her.
Rav Naḥman bar Pappa's seeds failed to grow until he prayed for mercy, resulting in rain and successful sprouting.
Rav Ḥisda instructs Rav Taḥlifa to record and explain specific terms in his book of aggada.
A duck in Mar Shmuel's house had a gizzard that wouldn't peel until they placed it in the sun to soften it.
Rav Adda bar Shimi challenges a tradition about the raḥam bird by citing an incident where one hissed in a field and was immediately killed by a falling stone.
Ravina asks his mother to hide worms in his fish so he can eat it, leading to a legal challenge from Rav Mesharshiyya.
Avimi arrives from Bei Ḥozai carrying a baraita to challenge the current legal discourse.
Ulla rebukes Rav Yehuda's challenge by expressing extreme reverence for the deceased Rav and Shmuel while maintaining his own legal position.
While Rav Yosef is reciting traditions before Rav Huna, a colleague challenges his accuracy, leading Rav Yosef to react in anger before explaining the legal distinction that resolves the conflict.
When Rabbi Zeira arrives in Eretz Yisrael, Rav Asi confirms his teaching but describes how Resh Lakish once sat in silence waiting for Rabbi Yohanan to retract, leaving his own opinion unknown.
Adda bar Havu seeks counsel from Rav Ashi after a bear attacks his unique animal, and Rav Ashi instructs him to slaughter it immediately to ensure it remains kosher.
Rav Yehuda is silenced by Ulla in a legal debate, but after Ulla leaves, Rav Yehuda reflects on why he didn't offer a specific resolution and concludes his silence was justified.
An anonymous sage offers a stringent ruling while sitting before Rabbi Abba, who then instructs his students to ignore the ruling.
Rav Ya'akov recalls the measurement used in Rav Yehuda's study hall regarding the convergence of sinews.
Mar bar Rav Ashi recalls standing before his father when a bird was brought for inspection and Rav Ashi examined its sinews.
Ulla cites an incident where Rabbi Yitzḥak brought a fledgling with a broken leg to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who ruled it kosher because the skin and flesh combined to cover the bone.
A case of soft sinews covering a broken bone was brought before Rabba, who ruled the animal permitted.
When Abaye delays ruling on a broken animal bone for three festivals, Rav Adda bar Mattana directs the owner to Rava, who provides a swift decision.
Rabbi Abba instructs his servant to carefully match the physical characteristics of mules before hitching them to his wagon to ensure they are of the same maternal species.
Rav Naḥman informs Rav Ashi that Ameimar actually permitted the consumption of the fat of forest goats, treating them as undomesticated animals.
Ya’akov the heretic challenges Rava regarding the covering of blood for domesticated animals, and Rava refutes him using a verse comparing blood to water.
Rav Eina teaches a law regarding covering blood on Shabbat at the Exilarch's gate, prompting Rabba to mock him and order his interpreter silenced.
Rabbi Ḥiyya seeks advice from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on how to deal with a moth infestation in his flax, and is told to slaughter a bird in a specific way to lure the pests away.
Rabbi Ami finds Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Zeira outside the study hall in Caesarea, leading Zeira to enter and engage with students regarding a legal dilemma.

Rav Beruna and Rav Hananel ask for a cup of wine to recite Grace, but when they change their minds and ask to drink more, Rav Yeiva the Elder rules that their first request already concluded the meal.
A heretic challenges Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and fails to find a rebuttal within three days, leading to the heretic's suicide and a celebratory meal for the Rabbi.
Jacob remains alone to retrieve small pitchers and is subsequently attacked by an angel who wrestles with him until dawn.
Rabbi Akiva recounts traveling with Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua to a meat market to buy animals for a wedding, where he posed a question to them.
The Gemara describes the differing physical practices of Rabba, Rabbi Yoḥanan, and Rabbi Asi regarding how they removed forbidden fat from kidneys.
Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya finds his son Levi instructing a worker to peel a spleen more stringently than necessary and rebukes him for it.
Shmuel becomes angry with his attendant after the attendant gives a deceptive gift to a ferryman while they are crossing a river.
Ulla visits Rav Yehuda, who opens wine barrels for him that had already been sold to a storekeeper.
A man mistakenly believes a gift of wine is oil due to a deceptive layer of oil on top, invites guests he cannot afford to host, and kills himself in shame upon discovering the truth.
During a famine, three guests give their meager portions to the host's son, leading to a series of misunderstandings that result in the deaths of the host, his wife, and his son.
Mar Zutra encounters Rava and Rav Safra on the road and mistakenly thinks they came to honor him, leading to a conflict over whether one should correct such a misconception.

A butcher taunts his fellow about not sharing meat, which reveals an incident of selling non-kosher meat to a gentile. A butcher taunts his friend for missing a meal, only to discover the friend ate the meat after the butcher improperly sold it to a gentile; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi then rules on the status of the city's meat markets based on this incident.

Rav is sitting by the river and observes a man washing an animal head, which then falls into the water. A man loses an animal head in a river and retrieves two, leading Rav to forbid both due to the uncertainty of their origin.
Rav visits his son-in-law and, after observing the meat through a door crack and seeing certain omens, refuses to eat the meal.
Rabbi Yohanan, impressed by Shmuel's wisdom, plans to visit him but cancels the trip after a child recites a verse he interprets as an omen of Shmuel's death.
On the eve of Yom Kippur, ravens drop meat, and Rav Kahana permits Rav Nahman to eat it.
Rav Hiyya bar Avin loses meat in a wine cellar and is permitted to eat it by Rav Huna after identifying it through visual recognition.
Rav Hanina Hoza'a loses a side of meat and is permitted to eat it by Rav Nahman based on visual recognition.
Rav Natan bar Abaye loses ritual blue wool and is permitted to use it by Rav Hisda after identifying it.

While Bar Peyoli was removing a sciatic nerve in front of Shmuel, Shmuel's sharp rebuke caused him to drop his knife in fear, leading Shmuel to reassure him that his practice followed a valid (though different) legal opinion.
Rav Huna presents a legal ruling regarding a kid roasted with its forbidden fat to challenge Shmuel's position on roasting.
An incident is recounted where a goat was roasted with forbidden fat in the synagogue of Maon, and Rabbi Yoḥanan was consulted to determine its permissibility.
When thighs were salted with the sciatic nerve in the Exilarch's house, Ravina and Rav Aha disagreed on their permissibility until Mar bar Rav Ashi ruled they were permitted.
When forbidden fat fell into a pot of meat, Rav Asi proposed measuring the pot's absorption toward the nullification ratio, but the Rabbis corrected him.
Mar bar Rav Ashi attempted to permit a mixture where fat fell into meat using a lower ratio, but his father, Rav Ashi, rebuked him and insisted on the standard measure.
A man brought a mixture to Rabban Gamliel, who ruled leniently by citing an even more lenient precedent from his father.
A man brought a mixture to Rabbi Shimon, who ruled based on his father's precedent using specific ratios.
A man brings a case to Rabbi Hiyya, who asks if there is a 1:30 ratio and prohibits it.
A man seeking a ruling on a sciatic nerve is sent back and forth between Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevina, who is sitting at the gate, leading to a sharp clarification from Rabbi Hanina.
Rav publicly challenges Rabba bar bar Hana's ruling by appointing a disseminator to announce a contrary position to the masses.

Rava explains a legal ruling by citing a historical incident where, due to religious persecution, a message was sent from the Land of Israel to inform the community that Yom Kippur would coincide with Shabbat.
Rabbi Elazar poses a legal question to Rabbi Asi specifically to remind him of a tradition Asi had forgotten, eventually prompting him by recalling how Asi used to recite it before Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Rav Yitzḥak son of Rav Mesharshiyya visits Rav Ashi and eats meat immediately after cheese without washing his hands, defending his behavior to the household by distinguishing between day and night.
Abaye patrols his property and catches his sharecropper attempting to steal wood by claiming it was for Abaye's own house.
Rav Asi, while patrolling his property, discovers a flood and uses his own cloak to plug the breach, realizing the value of his vigilance.
An angel of poverty tries to catch a man being careless with crumbs on grass, but the man outsmarts him by uprooting the grass and throwing it into the river.
Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna engage in a magical duel with a matron who stops their boat after they refuse her a ride.
Mar bar Rav Ashi summons and successfully sues a demon for breaking a barrel of wine belonging to porters.

A demon serving in Rav Pappa's house explains his delay in fetching water by describing the 'foul waters' he had to wait to pass. A demon servant in Rav Pappa's house observes the family pouring out water before drinking and remarks that had he known they did this, he wouldn't have delayed his trips to the river.
Rav Dimi reports an incident where a storekeeper served pig meat to a Jew because the Jew's failure to wash his hands led the storekeeper to believe he was a gentile.
A failure to wash hands after a meal (final waters) leads to a host's wife being tricked by guests and subsequently killed by her husband.
Rabba bar bar Hana observes Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi eating fruit without washing their hands and notes they did not offer him any.
Bar Hedya reports standing before Rabbi Ami and witnessing him indicate the proper hand-washing measurement for a legal ruling.
Rav Ya’akov and Rav Ashi each prepared specific vessels of a certain volume for washing their hands.
Rabbi Tzadok is given a small amount of food and chooses to eat it with a cloth outside of the Sukka.

Shmuel encounters Rav eating bread with his hands wrapped in a cloth and questions him. Shmuel finds Rav eating with a cloth instead of washing his hands, and Rav explains he does so because he is physically delicate.
Rabbi Zeira arrives in Eretz Yisrael and discovers Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi eating with their hands wrapped in wineskin scraps, leading to a confrontation about the legality of the practice.
Rav Huna bar Seḥora feeds a piece of meat directly to Rav Hamnuna while the latter is standing before him.
Shmuel's father finds him crying because his teacher struck him for feeding a child without washing his hands; the father defends Shmuel, noting the teacher's legal error.
Rabbi Elazar instructs his attendant to tear an udder before roasting it so that he may eat it.
Yalta argues to her husband Rav Nachman that for every forbidden item there is a permitted equivalent, leading him to order his cooks to roast udders for her to provide the taste of meat and milk.
Passage B is a distinct narrative involving Rabbi Elazar, Ze'eiri, and Rav Yitzḥak bar Avudimi investigating the origins of Rav's ruling, whereas Passage A is the actual event of Rav in Tatlefush.
Rav arrives in Tatlefush, overhears a woman asking how much milk is needed to cook meat, and decides to stay in the town to teach them the law.
Ravin and Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef are served udder at Rav Pappi's house; Rav Yitzḥak eats it while Ravin refuses, prompting a comment from Abaye.

Rami bar Tamrei visits Sura and eats udders, leading the locals to bring him to Rav Ḥisda's court where he defends his unconventional behavior and lack of ritual garments. While Rav Hisda is questioning Rami bar Tamrei, a man is brought to court to be flogged for not honoring his parents, but Rami bar Tamrei intervenes by citing a baraita that limits the court's power to punish for that specific commandment.
Abaye asks Rav Safra to inquire about liver preparation in Eretz Yisrael, and upon his return, they discuss the legal implications of the answer received.
Rav Safra returns to Eretz Yisrael and asks Rabbi Zerika about cooking liver, who responds by describing a visit he made to the house of Yehuda.
Rav bar Shabba visits Rav Naḥman and refuses to eat the liver served to him, leading Rav Naḥman to call him haughty.
While visiting Rabba bar Rav Naḥman, Rabba bar Rav Huna discovers improperly prepared liver and instructs the household on how to correctly tear the arteries.

Rav Ashi visits his father-in-law and observes his brother-in-law roasting liver on top of meat. Rav Ashi visits his father-in-law and rebukes his brother-in-law for roasting liver on top of meat, calling the practice haughty.
Abaye cites an incident where a bowl in Rabbi Ami's house cracked after salting meat, revealing absorbed blood.
Rav visits his grandson, receives eye treatment in a bowl, and subsequently refuses to eat ginger served in that same bowl.
Shmuel eats fish served in a meat bowl with dairy and offers some to Rabbi Elazar, who refuses because his own teacher (Rav) would not permit it.
Rav Huna and Rav Hiyya bar Ashi, sitting on opposite sides of a river, mock each other's religious practices during their meals.
A young bird falls into a jug of kutaḥ, and Rav Hinnana permits it, earning praise from Rava for his discernment.
The Gemara describes how Shmuel would throw bread contaminated by meat-blood to his dog, while Rav Huna would give it to his attendant.
Rav Mari bar Raḥel accidentally salted kosher meat with tereifa meat and brought the case to Rava, who ruled the kosher meat prohibited.
Rav Sheshet used to salt his meat one piece at a time.
Levi is served a peacock cooked in milk at the home of a bird hunter and remains silent, later explaining to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that he deferred to the local ruling of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak arrives in Babylonia from Eretz Yisrael and reports Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling regarding curdling milk with rennet.
A certain elder approaches Rabbi Elazar to resolve a legal dilemma by citing a tradition from Rabbi Yoḥanan regarding the validity of slaughter for impurity.
Passage B is a distinct narrative encounter between Rav Nahman and Ulla in Babylonia, which Passage A later references and recounts as a past event when Rav Oshaya travels to Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Oshaya travels to Eretz Yisrael and debates Rabbi Ami over the correct context of a ruling by Rabbi Yohanan, a dispute eventually clarified by the arrival of Ravin.
When Rav Avya the Elder asks a difficult question, Rabba bar Rav Huna distracts him by pointing at a raven because he is too exhausted from his public lecture to answer.

Rav Huna bar Torta witnesses the people of Va’ad crossbreeding a snake and a lizard, resulting in the birth of a dangerous arvad, which Rabbi Shimon the Righteous explains as a divine measure-for-measure punishment.

Passage B and Passage A are two distinct historical testimonies by Rabbi Yehuda regarding Rabbi Akiva's shifting halakhic positions, each involving different subject matter and concluding with a change in Akiva's ruling.
Rabbi Yehuda recounts how he challenged Rabbi Akiva's ruling on fat by citing Akiva's own teaching on endives, leading Akiva to retract and change his position.
Rabbi Asi misses a session at the study hall, encounters Rabbi Zeira, and asks him to review the day's teachings to help resolve a legal difficulty.
A Levite was snatching priestly gifts from children, and when Rav was informed, he rebuked the Levite's greed while noting the legal complexity of taxing Levites.
Ulla habitually gives priestly gifts to the daughters of priests, prompting Rava to challenge the legality of this practice using a baraita regarding meal offerings.
Several rabbis are noted for eating priestly gifts by virtue of being married to daughters of priests.
A priest follows Rabbi Tavla's advice to enter a partnership to avoid priestly gifts, but Rav Nahman rejects the arrangement and rebukes Rabbi Tavla for his ruling.
Rava and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak fined individuals who refused to give priestly gifts by seizing their property.
Abaye recounts how he transitioned from seizing priestly gifts to refusing them entirely after learning the proper ethical and legal conduct for priests.
Rava and Rav Safra visit a host where Rava eats priestly gifts against a general ruling; Rav Safra receives a rebuking dream which Rav Yosef later explains was actually intended for Rava.
Levi sowed crops in Kishar and, finding no poor people to collect the gleanings, consulted Rav Sheshet on how to proceed.
When a sack of coins was brought to the study hall for students, Rabbi Ami rushed to take it for himself (or for distribution).
Upon arriving in Eretz Yisrael, Isi bar Hini is corrected by Rabbi Yoḥanan regarding his terminology and his disrespectful manner of referring to the sage Rav.
Rav Kahana recounts seeing rows of pigeons calling out to their master, including an exchange where one pigeon rebukes another for remaining silent.
Rav Yehuda flogs a man who clipped a mother bird's wings before sending it away and orders him to let the wings grow back so he can fulfill the mitzva correctly.
A man asks Rava about the status of a specific bird, and after the man releases it to fulfill the mitzva, Rava uses nets to catch it for himself.
Levi bar Simon transfers his dovecote produce to Rav Yehuda, who then consults Shmuel on how to legally acquire them, leading Shmuel to tell him to bang on the nest.
A son obeys his father's request to collect fledglings, performs the mitzvah of sending away the mother bird, but falls to his death upon descending.
